strengths: Addresses a practically important problem — reducing visual token count for VLM video understanding under latency/memory constraints — and reports substantial efficiency gains (72% GPU memory reduction, ~24% latency reduction).

The retrieve-then-compress pipeline (event-based segmentation + query-relevant retrieval, followed by temporal token merging and RL-based distillation) is a reasonable and intuitively motivated design that combines ideas from Video-RAG and token-merging literature.

Extensive empirical evaluation across six diverse benchmarks (both video reasoning and general video QA) with several baselines and models (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3.5, Gemma-3, ByteVideoLLM, MovieChat, VidCom2).
Reasonably thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of VMR alone, C-GRPO alone, comparison against SFT/SFT+VMR, and sensitivity to the retention threshold τ.
The reported result of near-baseline mean accuracy (42.20 vs 42.21) with ~95% token reduction is an appealing headline number if the underlying evaluation is sound.
weaknesses: The core novelty of C-GRPO is limited: it is essentially GRPO with an added scalar retention-ratio bonus gated by a correctness indicator (Eq. 7-8); the technical contribution beyond reward engineering is thin relative to the claim of being a fundamentally new RL strategy.

Fairness of baseline comparisons is questionable: MARC benefits from the VMR retrieval stage (which alone raises mean score from 42.21 to 45.56, Table 2) while competing compression baselines (ByteVideoLLM, MovieChat, VidCom2) are not given the same retrieval-augmented input; this conflates the gains from retrieval versus the RL compression algorithm and makes the reported large margins (65%, 31%, 52%) potentially misleading.

The paper glosses over the degraded performance on long-video benchmarks (VideoMME retains only 74% of baseline performance with 3.21% of tokens), which is arguably the most stringent test of the method (long, information-dense video, single-frame-equivalent budget). This weakens the central claim of "nearly identical" performance under extreme compression.

τ ablation differences (41.34 vs 42.20 vs 41.40, Table 3) are small and no variance/multiple-seed results are reported anywhere, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported gains.

Potential data leakage/overlap is not addressed: the training data (Video-R1-260K) is drawn from public video datasets that may overlap in source videos or distributions with the evaluation benchmarks (e.g., MVBench, VideoMME components), which is not discussed or controlled for.

Insufficient detail/clarity on the teacher-student training loop: it is unclear whether the teacher network is frozen, how afull (teacher reward) is computed at each training step (added compute cost), and how compute-heavy the 64-frame teacher rollout is during RL training — reproducibility is weak given these gaps plus reliance on an unincluded appendix (with a broken "Appendix ??" reference).
Only a single model scale (3B) and one backbone (Qwen2.5-VL) is used for the main method; no results on larger models or alternative backbones to demonstrate generality of the approach.

The elaborate cognitive-science motivation (episodic memory, event segmentation theory, neuroimaging) is not tightly connected to concrete algorithmic choices beyond standard shot-boundary detection and embedding-based retrieval, giving an impression of overclaiming conceptual novelty relative to the actual technical mechanism.
No qualitative analysis, failure case discussion, or error analysis is provided to help understand when/why the compression succeeds or fails, particularly on the weaker VideoMME results.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: reducing the massive token overhead of VLMs when extended to long/high-fps video, with a clear efficiency motivation (latency, GPU memory) for real-world deployment.

The retrieve-then-compress pipeline (event-based segmentation + embedding retrieval, followed by a memory-aware temporal merge) is a reasonable combination of existing ideas and is evaluated on six diverse benchmarks spanning both video reasoning and general video understanding.

Reported efficiency numbers (72% GPU memory reduction, ~24% latency reduction, 95% token reduction) are compelling if they hold up, and the paper includes some supporting ablations (effect of VMR alone, SFT baseline comparison, sensitivity to the threshold τ).
The idea of coupling a retention-ratio-based reward to GRPO to explicitly preserve teacher-level performance under compression is an intuitive and conceptually reasonable mechanism.
weaknesses: The central claim of compressing a video down to the token-equivalent of 'a single frame' is not clearly reconciled with the VMR procedure, which retrieves top-k=3 multi-frame event segments at 1fps; the paper never clearly explains how multiple retrieved segments collapse to ~1 frame's worth of tokens (122.69 tokens), making a key quantitative headline claim under-specified and hard to verify.

The core RL contribution (C-GRPO) is a fairly incremental modification of GRPO (adding a correctness-gated retention-ratio bonus term); no ablation isolates this specific reward component against vanilla GRPO with the same compressed input — the only RL-related ablation sweeps τ, which does not establish whether the retention reward itself is necessary versus standard GRPO/distillation losses.

The comparison against SFT as the sole strong baseline for assessing C-GRPO's value is a weak/strawman comparison; RL-based distillation should instead be compared against more standard alternatives such as plain knowledge distillation losses, vanilla GRPO without the compression reward, or other RL-based compression baselines, none of which are included.

Training-time costs are not reported or discussed: C-GRPO requires running both a 64-frame teacher and single-frame student per rollout per group (G=8), which is computationally expensive; the paper only reports inference-time efficiency gains, giving an incomplete picture of total cost/benefit.

VMR's own computational overhead (event segmentation via TransNetV2, embedding-based retrieval, nearest-neighbor search) is not factored into the reported latency/memory numbers, which could meaningfully offset claimed efficiency gains, especially for the 'real-time' deployment scenarios emphasized in the abstract.

Performance on VideoMME (the long-video benchmark) retains only 74% of baseline accuracy while using 3.21% of tokens, which is a substantial drop that is understated in the abstract's 'nearly identical accuracy' framing — an instance of selectively emphasizing favorable aggregate numbers while underselling a benchmark where the method struggles most (arguably the most relevant benchmark for genuinely long videos).

Naming inconsistencies and apparent errors (e.g., 'ByteVideoLLM' in Table 1 vs. 'DynamicVLM' in the text discussion, a broken 'Appendix ??' reference) suggest insufficient proofreading and reduce confidence in other reported details.

The cognitive-science/neuroimaging motivation for the Visual Memory Retriever is largely rhetorical; the actual implementation (TransNetV2 shot-boundary detection + off-the-shelf embedding retrieval) is standard retrieval machinery and not clearly grounded in or validated against the cited neuroscience principles, amounting to overclaiming in the framing.

Evaluation is confined to a single 3B-parameter backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) for the proposed method; no results demonstrate that MARC/C-GRPO generalizes to other backbones or larger models, limiting evidence for the generality of the approach despite comparisons against other models' baseline numbers.

No statistical significance testing, variance across seeds, or multiple-run reporting is provided, which is particularly important given RL training's known instability and the paper's reliance on a single τ value selected post-hoc via the same benchmarks used for final evaluation (risk of overfitting hyperparameter choice to the test sets).

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem of reducing visual token count for video LLMs under tight latency/memory budgets, with a clearly motivated retrieve-then-compress pipeline.

The combination of an event-level Visual Memory Retriever with an RL-based distillation objective (C-GRPO) that explicitly couples student performance to a full-frame teacher via a retention-ratio reward is a reasonably novel idea beyond standard training-free token merging.

Evaluation spans six diverse benchmarks covering both video reasoning and general understanding, and the paper reports concrete efficiency numbers (72% GPU memory reduction, ~24% latency reduction, 95% token reduction), which are useful for practitioners.
Reasonable set of ablations are included: effect of VMR alone, SFT vs. C-GRPO comparison, and a sweep over the retention threshold τ, which help attribute gains to different components.

Comparisons against several training-free compression baselines (MovieChat, VidCom2, ByteVideoLLM/DynamicVLM) under a matched token budget provide some evidence of superiority over naive compression heuristics.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'nearly identical' performance to the 64-frame baseline is supported mainly by an unweighted mean across heterogeneous benchmarks; on VideoMME (arguably the most realistic long-video benchmark) the method only retains ~74% of baseline accuracy while using 3.21% of the tokens, which is a substantial degradation that the aggregate mean obscures.

All core experiments use a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B); the other VLMs (InternVL3.5, Gemma-3) are shown only as plain uncompressed baselines, not integrated with MARC, so generalization of the method across architectures/model scales is unverified.

The retrieval pipeline (TransNetV2 event segmentation + a separate embedding/retrieval model) introduces non-trivial additional inference-time computation (segmentation, embedding, nearest-neighbor search) that is not accounted for in the reported latency/memory comparisons, making the efficiency claims potentially optimistic.

Key design choices (top-k=3 for VMR, window size m for temporal merging, reward scaling α, group size G=8) are not systematically ablated beyond τ, leaving it unclear how sensitive results are to these hyperparameters or how they were tuned, raising reproducibility concerns.

No variance/multiple-seed reporting is provided for RL training, which is known to be unstable; a single-run comparison between SFT, SFT+VMR, and C-GRPO is insufficient to establish robustness of the claimed gains.

The SFT baseline comparison uses a different, smaller data subset (10K vs. 5K for C-GRPO as stated, with some inconsistency) and the implementation details are deferred entirely to the appendix, making the comparison difficult to independently judge as fair.

Some claims are overstated, e.g., calling C-GRPO 'the first' RL strategy for video token compression without a thorough discussion of closely related RL-based distillation/compression work, and the cognitive-science motivation for VMR is asserted but not empirically validated against simpler segmentation/retrieval alternatives.

Minor presentation issues (e.g., a broken cross-reference 'Appendix ??', reliance on appendices for essential implementation details) suggest the manuscript could benefit from another revision pass before being fully convincing for a top-tier venue.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem—reducing token counts for video-LLMs—with a comprehensive efficiency evaluation (72% GPU memory reduction, 23.9% latency reduction) that is grounded in real measurements on a single GPU.
Evaluation spans six diverse benchmarks covering both reasoning and general video understanding, giving a reasonably broad picture of performance retention under compression.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies: effect of the retention threshold τ, isolated contribution of VMR vs. C-GRPO, and comparison against an SFT-based distillation baseline, which helps disentangle the two proposed components.

The retrieve-then-compress pipeline is intuitively motivated and the reported near-parity mean score (42.20 vs 42.21) against a 64-frame baseline while using ~5% of the tokens is an appealing headline result if it generalizes.
Reasonable coverage of related training-free and RAG-style compression baselines in Section 2, situating the contribution within the literature.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited: VMR is essentially standard shot-segmentation + embedding retrieval (existing off-the-shelf components: TransNet v2 and a pretrained embedding model), and C-GRPO is GRPO plus a simple correctness-gated retention-ratio bonus—an incremental reward-shaping addition rather than a fundamentally new RL algorithm.

The formulation of the compression reward is underspecified: it is unclear how a_full and a_comp (average rewards under 64-frame vs. compressed input) are computed per training step/batch, whether the teacher is run online for every sample, and how this interacts with GRPO's group-relative advantage estimation—this hampers reproducibility.

Headline 'near-identical mean performance' obscures large disparities across benchmarks: MARC retains only 74% of baseline performance on VideoMME (long videos) while exceeding baseline on some short-video benchmarks; averaging masks this failure mode and the paper's framing somewhat overstates general applicability.

Comparisons to prior compression methods are inconsistent/confusing: the text says the method is compared to 'DynamicVLM' but Table 1 and its caption list 'ByteVideoLLM' instead, suggesting possible errors in reporting or result attribution.

Missing comparisons to well-known, more competitive recent training-free/training-based token compression baselines (e.g., FastV, VisionZip, PruMerge, SparseVLM, which are even cited in the related work) — only three relatively weaker baselines are actually benchmarked.

VMR relies on pre-indexing/embedding an entire video corpus before retrieval, which appears to conflict with the paper's stated real-time/streaming applications (autonomous driving, surveillance) where the whole video is not available in advance.

No variance/seed information, statistical significance testing, or robustness analysis (e.g., different top-k, different backbones) is reported, and the method is validated only on a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B), limiting evidence of generality.

The cognitive-science motivation for VMR (episodic memory, event segmentation theory) is largely decorative narrative rather than a substantive mechanistic connection reflected in the actual algorithm, which is a standard retrieval + merge pipeline.

Minor writing/consistency issues (e.g., duplicate 'SuperCLEVR' in appendix lists, inconsistent baseline naming) suggest the manuscript would benefit from a more careful proofreading and result-table cross-check pass.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: reducing visual token counts for efficient video-LLM inference under resource constraints.

Combines a retrieval mechanism (VMR) with an RL-based distillation objective (C-GRPO) in a reasonably coherent pipeline, and provides ablations isolating the contribution of each component (VMR alone, SFT vs C-GRPO, τ sensitivity).
Reports concrete efficiency numbers (72% GPU memory reduction, ~24% latency reduction) alongside accuracy, which is useful for practitioners.

Evaluates on six diverse benchmarks spanning reasoning and general video understanding, and compares against several training-free compression baselines (MovieChat, VidCom, ByteVideoLLM) reproduced under a matched token budget.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'nearly identical accuracy with 95% fewer tokens' is overstated: on VideoMME (long videos, arguably the most compression-relevant setting), the method retains only ~74% of baseline performance, yet this major degradation is relegated to an appendix 'failure case' discussion rather than reflected in the abstract/intro claims.

The efficiency analysis (Fig. 5) appears to omit the computational cost of the VMR pipeline itself (event segmentation network, embedding model, nearest-neighbor retrieval), which is non-trivial for long videos; without this accounting, the reported latency/memory savings are not a fair end-to-end comparison.

The gains attributed to 'compression' are confounded with gains from smarter clip selection: Table 2 shows VMR alone (no compression, no training) already beats the 64-frame uniform baseline by a wide margin (45.56 vs 42.21), suggesting much of MARC's improvement stems from fixing a weak uniform-sampling baseline rather than from genuine token-compression efficacy.

C-GRPO is a fairly incremental modification of standard GRPO (adding a correctness-gated retention-ratio bonus term); the technical novelty is limited, and the paper provides no training dynamics, reward curves, or analysis of potential reward hacking beyond a qualitative claim that gating 'reduces' it.

Baseline comparisons mix different frame/token budgets and model families (e.g., comparing MARC-3B against InternVL3.5-4B and Gemma-3-4B using full 64-frame inputs) without controlling for backbone capability, training data, or instruction-tuning recipe, weakening the validity of 'MARC beats larger models' claims.

Only a single training-based baseline (SFT) is compared; no comparison to other RL-based or learned frame-selection/compression methods in the literature, limiting positioning relative to the state of the art.
Training uses only 5K samples with no reported variance across seeds/runs for an RL method known to have high training variance, raising reproducibility and robustness concerns.

The retrieve-then-compress design is only validated with top-k=3 fixed clip retrieval; the appendix's own failure analysis shows this breaks down for videos with many clips (VideoMME, VideoMMMU), and no adaptive mechanism is proposed or evaluated to address it, despite being flagged as a core limitation.

Figures and some reported numbers (e.g., token counts in Fig. 4 appear inconsistent with values in Table 4) and generic/boilerplate ethics and reproducibility statements reduce confidence in the paper's polish and care.

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem (video token compression for VLMs) with a well-motivated retrieve-then-compress pipeline.

Combines a segmentation+retrieval module (VMR) with a novel RL-based distillation objective (C-GRPO) that explicitly ties the compressed-model reward to retention of teacher-level performance, which is a reasonable technical idea beyond prior training-free token merging.

Evaluation spans six diverse benchmarks (reasoning and general video understanding) and reports consistent efficiency gains (72% GPU memory reduction, ~24% latency reduction) alongside near-parity accuracy versus a 64-frame baseline using only ~4.7% of the tokens.
Reasonably thorough ablations: comparison to SFT and SFT+VMR, sensitivity of the retention threshold τ, and isolation of VMR's contribution versus C-GRPO's contribution.
Honest discussion of failure modes (long-video degradation on VideoMME), including plausible explanation tied to clip count and retrieval top-k limitations.
Efficiency numbers are measured empirically (not just theoretical FLOPs), including GPU memory and latency breakdowns.
weaknesses: All experiments use a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B); no evidence the VMR+C-GRPO framework generalizes to other model families or larger scales, despite the paper positioning this as a general-purpose compression framework.

Baseline token-compression methods (ByteVideoLLM, MovieChat, VidCom) are self-reproduced on Qwen2.5-VL-3B rather than compared via their original released checkpoints/implementations where possible, raising fairness/reproducibility concerns about whether these reproductions are representative of the original methods' best performance.

The retention-ratio reward (η = a_comp/a_full) requires running a 64-frame teacher forward pass during RL training for every sample; the added training-time computational cost of this teacher rollout is not reported or discussed, undermining the 'efficiency' narrative which focuses only on inference.

The novelty of C-GRPO is somewhat incremental: it is essentially standard GRPO with an additional correctness-gated reward term comparing compressed vs. uncompressed rewards; the core RL machinery (clipping, KL penalty, group-normalized advantages) is unchanged from Shao et al. 2024.

Performance on long videos (VideoMME) drops substantially (only 74% retention), and the proposed explanation (clip count explosion for long videos limiting top-k retrieval) suggests the method may not scale well to genuinely long-form video, a core motivating use case mentioned in the abstract (surveillance, autonomous driving).

Training data for C-GRPO is quite small (5K samples, further restricted to top-3 VMR clips), raising questions about robustness and statistical reliability of reported ablation differences (e.g., τ=0.4 vs 0.6 vs 0.8 differences of ~1 point may not be significant); no variance/multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in the paper.

The VMR module's own computational/latency overhead (event segmentation network + embedding/retrieval) is not clearly isolated in the efficiency comparison (Figure 5); it's unclear whether reported memory/latency savings account for this preprocessing cost.

Minor clarity issues: frequent interchangeable/inconsistent use of 'VLM' and 'vLLM', and some claims (e.g., 'first post-training RL strategy specifically designed for video token compression') are not rigorously substantiated against the broader RL-for-compression literature.

Code and model links are placeholders in the submission, and no demonstration of actual release is provided, which combined with limited hyperparameter/architecture detail (e.g., VMR embedding model specifics, segmentation thresholds) makes full reproducibility uncertain.
